record.title: THAW-VLA distills world-model features into a compact robot policy
record.summary: THAW-VLA uses a frozen world model to produce cached training-frame features, then adds a feature-alignment loss to a compact vision-language-action policy. The teacher and projector are removed before deployment, so inference uses the undistilled student graph. The authors report a 0.8B policy moving from 95.3% to 97.9% mean success on LIBERO and from 48.2% to 50.5% on RoboCasa-GR1; they also report gains over the same student on single-arm and bimanual real-robot tasks, with 30 trials per cell. A single RTX 5090 profile is reported at 32 ms and 1.86 GB. Results remain author-reported and task-specific; independent reproduction and broader robot/task coverage are open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: THAW-VLA trains a compact vision-language-action student with a feature-alignment loss against cached representations from a frozen world model; the teacher and projection head are removed at deployment.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report a 0.8B student improving LIBERO mean success from 95.3% to 97.9% and RoboCasa-GR1 success from 48.2% to 50.5%, against the same student trained without feature alignment.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On two real-robot platforms and three manipulation tasks, the authors report 30 trials per cell and gains over the undistilled student; the 0.8B policy is reported at 32 ms per inference and 1.86 GB GPU memory on an RTX 5090.

contradictory_evidence: The reported LIBERO improvement is modest in absolute terms (95.3% to 97.9%) and comes from a high-performing benchmark regime; it does not establish broad robustness.
The project page notes remaining real-robot failures are placement errors and reports only selected pick-and-place/handover tasks.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of simulation, real-robot success, latency or memory measurements was conducted.
Generalization across unseen robot platforms, task families, visual conditions and deployment hardware is not measured in the reviewed result tables.
The additional offline compute and storage required to generate/cache world-model features are not included in the latency/memory comparison.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported transfer generalizes, a compact robot policy could gain measurable task performance from a world model without paying its seconds-per-decision inference cost, changing practical deployment tradeoffs for embodied systems. Consequence is meaningful but bounded to a 0.8B student, selected manipulation tasks and author-reported results.
limitations: All reported results are author-run and were not independently reproduced by this review.
The real-robot results cover two platforms, three manipulation tasks and 30 trials per cell; they do not establish broad transfer across robots, environments or task families.
Some table baselines are quoted from prior papers with different protocols; the strongest within-paper comparison is the same student without feature alignment.
The latency and memory figures are one RTX 5090 profile; energy, training cost and performance on other hardware are not established.
LIBERO simulation gains are 2.6 percentage points in the reported mean; task-level variation and benchmark saturation matter.
brief.summary: THAW-VLA uses a frozen world model to produce cached training-frame features, then adds a feature-alignment loss to a compact vision-language-action policy. The teacher and projector are removed before deployment, so inference uses the undistilled student graph. The authors report a 0.8B policy moving from 95.3% to 97.9% mean success on LIBERO and from 48.2% to 50.5% on RoboCasa-GR1; they also report gains over the same student on single-arm and bimanual real-robot tasks, with 30 trials per cell. A single RTX 5090 profile is reported at 32 ms and 1.86 GB. Results remain author-reported and task-specific; independent reproduction and broader robot/task coverage are open.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report LIBERO mean success 95.3% to 97.9%, RoboCasa-GR1 48.2% to 50.5%, selected real-robot task improvements, and 32 ms / 1.86 GB inference.
technical.compute_or_cost: The authors report 32 ms and 1.86 GB for inference on an RTX 5090. The offline world-model feature precompute cost, cache size and full training cost are not quantified in the reviewed page.
technical.demonstrated_result: No independent demonstration by this review. The project page reports the method, same-student controls, result tables and trial counts.
technical.implementation_status: The project page links source code and checkpoints; this review inspected the page and arXiv report but did not run the repository.
technical.mechanism: Run a frozen world model over training frames once, cache its internal visual features, and train the student VLA with an added cosine feature-alignment loss. Remove the world model and projector after training; deploy the ordinary student policy graph.
technical.novelty: Transfers a world-model representation prior into a compact VLA during training while leaving the deployed policy architecture and inference graph unchanged.
technical.regime: 0.8B Qwen-based VLA student. LIBERO results average four evaluation runs (2 seeds × 2 GPUs); RoboCasa-GR1 results include a four-run comparison and additional single-run ablations; real-robot results cover an AgileX Nero and TRIP-Bag with 30 trials per cell. Inference profile uses one RTX 5090.
technical.reproducibility: The paper and project page provide model/task details and public links; exact independent reruns, checkpoint provenance and full precompute/training economics were not verified here.
technical.strongest_baseline: The same student backbone trained on the same setup without the feature-alignment term. Comparisons with larger outside policies are contextual and not fully matched.

brief.title: THAW-VLA distills world-model features into a compact robot policy
brief.why_it_matters: The method transfers a world model’s scene representation into a smaller deployed policy without loading the world model or adding test-time generation. If reproduced across tasks and hardware, this could preserve some world-model grounding while reducing deployment latency and memory. Current evidence is an author-run benchmark suite and a small set of real-robot tasks.
